title: Pronunciation Problems of Vietnamese Learners of English
description: Why Vietnamese learners drop ending sounds and swap th, sh and tr, what the research counts, and a classroom fix for each sound, -s/-ed ending and stress.
h1: Pronunciation problems of Vietnamese learners of English, and a fix for each one
intro: The biggest pronunciation problem for Vietnamese learners of English is ending sounds. Vietnamese allows only six word-final consonants and no consonant clusters, so learners drop, swap or blur the ends of English words, including plural and third-person -s and past -ed. Next come th, sh and tr substitutions, then word stress and intonation carried over from tonal Vietnamese. The practical fix is short, regular drilling inside high-frequency phrases.
keyPoints: **The root cause is syllable shape:** Vietnamese allows only six word-final consonants (/m n ŋ p t k/) and no clusters, while English can end a word with most of its 24 consonants and stack up to four, as in 'twelfths' ([ICHUSO 2019 study](https://hs.kku.ac.th/ichuso/2019/034-ICHUSO-2019.pdf)).

**Ending sounds come first:** in a study of 51 graduating English majors at Vietnam National University, dropped final sounds were the most common error, made by 25 of them ([Ha Cam Tam](https://js.vnu.edu.vn/FS/article/view/2072)).

**-s goes missing a lot:** adult learners in a 2024 study dropped 28.4% of expected final /s/ and /z/, and about half of grammatical -s after a consonant, as in 'books' or 'wants' ([Disney & Le](https://www.mdpi.com/2226-471X/9/10/327)).

**The consonant swaps are predictable:** /θ/ becomes /t/ or /s/, /ð/ becomes /z/ or /d/, /ʃ/ and /s/ trade places, /tr/ becomes /tʃ/ and /r/ can become /z/, so minimal pairs on exactly those contrasts pay off.

**Stress is a timing problem more than a pitch problem:** in a study of English compound and phrase stress, learners hit pitch and loudness fairly well but not timing, so stretch stressed syllables and shrink weak ones.
**Little and often, without costing face:** a five-minute ending-sounds slot in every lesson, choral drilling before individuals, and correction through whole-class feedback.

sections.title: Why Vietnamese learners find English sounds hard

blocks.text: Most of the problems trace back to how syllables are built. Vietnamese allows only six consonants at the end of a word, /m n ŋ p t k/, plus two semivowels, and it has **no consonant clusters at all**. English can end a word with most of its 24 consonants and pile up to four at the end, as in 'twelfths' ([word-final consonant study, ICHUSO 2019](https://hs.kku.ac.th/ichuso/2019/034-ICHUSO-2019.pdf); [study of English consonant clusters](https://www.vjol.info.vn/index.php/tctbgd/article/download/99155/83692/)). So every English word ending in /s/, /z/, /v/, /d/ or a cluster asks a Vietnamese speaker for a syllable their first language never makes.

Ha Cam Tam's study of 51 graduating English majors at Vietnam National University found dropped ending sounds to be the most common error and traced it to exactly this: Vietnamese words are single syllables with no clusters ([VNU Journal of Foreign Studies](https://js.vnu.edu.vn/FS/article/view/2072)).

The second source is rhythm. Vietnamese is a tonal language, where pitch tells one word from another, and it has no word-level timing rules like English stress. A phonetic study of compound and phrase stress (a 'GREENhouse' against a 'green HOUSE') found that Vietnamese learners, beginners and advanced alike, hit English pitch and loudness targets fairly well but adapt imperfectly to English timing ([Nguyen & Ingram, ICSLP 2002](https://www.isca-archive.org/icslp_2002/nguyen02b_icslp.html)). The same authors' later paper in TESOL Quarterly (2005) looks at how prosody from tonal Vietnamese carries over into English word stress ([TIRF reference list](https://www.tirfonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Vietnamese-speakingLearnersOfEnglish_SelectedReferences_2June2025.docx)).

blocks.text: These are not beginner problems that fade on their own. Ha Cam Tam's subjects were about to graduate in English, and a study at a Mekong Delta university found learners with a lot of English experience and learners with little making **many of the same types of final-consonant error** ([ICHUSO 2019](https://hs.kku.ac.th/ichuso/2019/034-ICHUSO-2019.pdf)). The words most often mispronounced in the VNU study were everyday ones: job, country, centre, the, English and tradition.

blocks.text: In the VNU study, 25 of the 51 students dropped final /z/, /s/, /t/, /v/, /ks/ or /dʒ/, and 19 also dropped sounds in the middle of words, mostly inside clusters. The author's recommendation is simple: put the emphasis on ending and medial consonants ([Ha Cam Tam](https://js.vnu.edu.vn/FS/article/view/2072)).

Dropping is not the only error. The Mekong Delta study found learners deleting a final consonant, adding an extra vowel after it, devoicing it, leaving a final stop unreleased so it is barely audible, and swapping it for another sound. In that study, swapping was the most common error on single final consonants, followed by devoicing and unreleased stops, and cutting a cluster down was the most common error on clusters, so listen for wrong and weak endings as well as missing ones. The cost is meaning, not just accent: **without its final /n/, 'line' can be heard as 'lie', 'like' or 'light'** ([ICHUSO 2019](https://hs.kku.ac.th/ichuso/2019/034-ICHUSO-2019.pdf)).
A five-minute ending-sounds routine

items.title: Pick one ending per lesson
items.text: Choose a single target from the table, for example final /s/ after a consonant, and six to eight words or chunks from that day's material. Choose frequent ones: in the 2024 -s study, learners were more accurate on more frequent words ([Disney & Le](https://www.mdpi.com/2226-471X/9/10/327)).

items.title: Exaggerate, then bring it back to normal
items.text: Model the ending long and clearly released, have the class repeat it chorally, then shorten it to natural length. Exaggerating final releases and linking at first gives learners a target they can actually hear.

items.title: Link the ending into the next word
items.text: Put the word before a vowel so the ending starts the next syllable: 'he wants it' runs together as wan-tsit, 'she worked on it' as work-ton-it. That takes the sound out of the position Vietnamese does not allow.

items.title: Hear it before saying it
items.text: Read out one word from a minimal set (line, lie, light, like) and have students show which one on mini-whiteboards or with fingers. Only then ask them to produce the set.

items.title: Recycle the same chunks
items.text: Come back to the same chunks at the end of the lesson and at the start of the next one, and praise endings you hear in freer speaking.

blocks.text: The -s ending gets its own research. Disney and Le (2024) analysed real speech from 16 Vietnamese adult learners and found they left out **28.4% of expected word-final /s/ and /z/**. Omission was most likely for grammatical -s after a consonant, plurals and third-person verbs, where the error rate was about 50.7%, and inside clusters. The authors conclude that first-language transfer alone does not explain the pattern, and how frequent a word is went closely with how accurately it was said ([Languages, MDPI](https://www.mdpi.com/2226-471X/9/10/327)). In practice: treat -s as grammar and sound together, and drill it in high-frequency phrases rather than word lists.

Watch for the opposite error too. In the VNU study 13 of 51 students added an /s/ or /z/ where none belongs, such as a /z/ inside 'hobby' or 'peoples' for 'people' ([Ha Cam Tam](https://js.vnu.edu.vn/FS/article/view/2072)). Learners who have been drilled hard on endings can start adding them everywhere, so keep meaning in the drill.

blocks.text: None of these six endings fits a Vietnamese syllable, which is why they need steady practice rather than one explanation. Teach the three-way rule once, then switch to activities:

items: **Sorting:** verbs on cards go into /t/, /d/ and /ɪd/ columns, then students read each column aloud in chorus.
**Yesterday chains:** each student adds a past-tense action to a growing sentence ('Yesterday I walked, cooked and wanted…'), so the endings repeat many times.
**Third-person routines:** describe a classmate's day ('She gets up, brushes her teeth, takes the bus') with the -s endings stretched at first.
**Deliberate mistakes:** say 'two book' or 'yesterday I play' and let the class correct you, which practises hearing the ending without putting any student on the spot.

sections.title: th, sh, tr, v, z and r: the consonant swaps

blocks.text: The VNU study counted these substitutions among its 51 students: /tr/ to /tʃ/ (16 students), /ʃ/ to /s/ (15), /t/ to /tʃ/ (13), /dʒ/ to various sounds (13), /s/ to /ʃ/ or /ʒ/ (11), /ð/ to /z/ or /d/ (10) and /θ/ to /s/ or /t/ (7). **/θ/ topped the list of mispronounced sounds**, usually produced as a t made against the teeth ([Ha Cam Tam](https://js.vnu.edu.vn/FS/article/view/2072)).
th: /θ/ and /ð/

Show the mouth: the tongue tip rests lightly between the teeth and air flows over it. Without voice it is /θ/ (think, three, month); add voice and it is /ð/ (the, this, they). Use triplets that hold everything else steady, such as think, tink and sink, or then, den and Zen. Because 'the' was among the most frequently mispronounced words in the VNU study, practise it inside chunks students say every day: 'in the morning', 'on the table', 'at the weekend'.
sh and s: /ʃ/ and /s/

The swap runs both ways, so the problem is telling the two apart rather than making either sound. Drill pairs in both directions: she and see, ship and sip, sheet and seat, shoe and Sue. For /ʃ/ the lips round and push forward; for /s/ they spread into a slight smile, which students can check in a mirror.
tr and t: /tr/ and /t/

Both /tr/ and plain /t/ can drift towards ch /tʃ/, so 'train' sounds like 'chain' and 'tip' like 'chip'. Contrast trip and chip, true and chew, tip and chip, and model a short, crisp /t/ released before the /r/ starts. Exaggerate the gap between the two sounds at first, then close it.
v, z and r

/v/ and /z/ show up in the research mainly as **ending sounds**: both are in the list of finals most often dropped, and /z/ is also what /ð/ often turns into. Practise them where they cause trouble, at the ends of words: five, love, have, lives, goes, was. For /v/, the top teeth stay on the lower lip while the voice keeps buzzing; for /z/, students touch their throat to feel the buzz and contrast it with /s/ in pairs such as rice and rise, place and plays.

/r/ shows up too: in the VNU study 7 of 51 students said /r/ as /z/, and /r/ was among the sounds dropped in the middle of words ([Ha Cam Tam](https://js.vnu.edu.vn/FS/article/view/2072)). Where you hear it, use the same hear-then-say routine with pairs such as rip and zip, rest and zest, and keep the tongue tip curled back without touching the roof of the mouth.

Nguyen and Ingram found that Vietnamese learners hit English pitch and loudness targets for stress fairly well, but adapt imperfectly to English timing, which Vietnamese has no equivalent rules for ([ICSLP 2002](https://www.isca-archive.org/icslp_2002/nguyen02b_icslp.html)). So the fix is mostly about **length**: the stressed syllable gets longer, and the unstressed ones shrink, often to a weak vowel. The same goes for small grammar words: in natural connected speech 'to', 'and', 'of', 'can' and 'for' are usually said in weak forms, so practise them that way.

Intonation can matter as much as the sounds. Luu Thi Kim Nhung (2010) argues that a wrong intonation contour can change what a Vietnamese learner means even when every consonant and vowel is correct, traces the likely problems to differences between the two intonation systems, and proposes teaching remedies ([VNU Journal of Foreign Studies](https://js.vnu.edu.vn/FS/article/view/2554)). A falling 'Really.' and a rising 'Really?' are different answers.

items: **Clap or hum** the stress pattern before saying the word, then say it with the stressed syllable deliberately long.
**Sort by pattern:** group new words under stress shapes such as Oo (teacher), oO (begin) and Ooo (family).
**Backchain** long sentences from the end: 'weekend', 'at the weekend', 'went out at the weekend', so the rhythm stays natural.
**Chunk sentences** into thought groups with a slash on the board, one stress per group.
**Hum the tune** of a question or a list first, then add the words; draw rising and falling arrows over model sentences.

blocks.text: This matters in exam classes. Vietnamese IELTS candidates averaged 6.2 overall in 2022 data, and Speaking was their weakest skill at 5.8 ([Viet Nam News](https://vietnamnews.vn/society/1638637/vietnamese-students-rank-23rd-globally-in-ielts-exam-annual-report.html)). The guide to [teaching IELTS in Vietnam](/teach-in-vietnam/teaching-ielts-in-vietnam) covers that market in detail.

sections.title: Correcting pronunciation without costing students face

blocks.text: Studies of Vietnamese learning culture report that students usually stay quiet and wait to be called on, and that face-saving is extremely important to students and their families ([Pham Thi My Hanh, NUS](https://fass.nus.edu.sg/cls/wp-content/uploads/sites/32/2020/10/pham_thimyhanh.pdf)). So correction works best when it does not single anyone out. The guide to [Vietnamese classroom culture](/teach-in-vietnam/vietnamese-classroom-culture-for-english-teachers) goes further into this.

items: **Drill chorally first,** then in groups, then in pairs, and only then call on individuals, by name and after some wait time.
**Correct through whole-class feedback:** note the errors you hear during speaking, then model and drill the right forms with everyone.
**Recast rather than interrupt** during fluency work: repeat the student's sentence back with the ending in place and move on.
**Use mini-whiteboards** for minimal-pair listening, so every student answers and no one is exposed.
**Praise in public,** especially the first time a quiet student gets an ending right in free speech.

blocks.title: Don't fix every ending mid-sentence
blocks.text: Stopping a student in front of the class to correct each dropped ending is an easy way to make a pronunciation focus backfire. It costs face, and quiet students go quieter. Save the correction for whole-class feedback and the next day's five-minute routine.

Class size shapes the method. Primary classes in Ho Chi Minh City averaged 38 pupils in 2022, above the legal cap of 35 ([VnExpress](https://vnexpress.net/truong-cong-qua-tai-4507502.html)), so public-school work leans on choral drilling, chants and actions. With young children, keep it physical and sound-based rather than symbol-based; the guide to [teaching young learners](/teach-in-vietnam/teaching-young-learners-in-vietnam) covers that age group. At a [language centre](/teach-in-vietnam/language-centre-jobs-in-ho-chi-minh-city), smaller groups leave room for pair work and individual feedback.

Two more things help. A short minimal-pair warm-up on ending sounds is a natural segment for a [demo lesson](/teach-in-vietnam/english-teacher-cv-and-demo-lesson-in-vietnam), because it shows you know these learners. And [learning some Vietnamese](/teach-in-vietnam/learning-vietnamese-and-finding-your-people-in-saigon) yourself makes the source of the errors easier to hear.

faqs.q: Should I aim to remove my students' Vietnamese accent?
faqs.a: No. Aim for intelligibility, not a native accent. Put the errors that change meaning or grammar first: dropped endings (line, lie, light), missing -s and -ed, and the th, sh and tr swaps.

faqs.q: Why do my advanced students still drop ending sounds?
faqs.a: The habit comes from Vietnamese syllable structure, which allows only six final consonants and no clusters, and research shows it persists at high levels: the VNU study's subjects were graduating English majors. Accuracy on -s also tracked how often a word is used, so drill endings in frequent phrases.

faqs.q: Should I teach phonemic symbols to Vietnamese students?
faqs.a: Many teachers find that, for teens and adults, a handful of symbols for the target sounds, such as the two th sounds, sh, s and z, makes minimal-pair work faster. Young learners need sounds, mouth shapes and actions rather than symbols. Check what your coursebook uses so you do not contradict it.
Yes. Pronunciation is one of the four criteria marked in the IELTS Speaking test, and Speaking was Vietnamese candidates' weakest skill in 2022 data, averaging 5.8 against 6.2 overall.

faqs.q: How much class time should pronunciation get?
faqs.a: There is no official figure. A short, regular slot of about five minutes in every lesson, recycling the same chunks, usually works better than an occasional full pronunciation lesson, because the habit being replaced is built into the learners' first language.
